g6-2023-014.quote: students use the order of operations to find the value of expressions
g6-2023-014.why: The item evaluates (3(7−2)+5^3)/2, which needs the parentheses, then the exponent, then the division. The Row Game is a column of numeric expressions with exponents that students evaluate by the order of operations, which is exactly the demand.

g6-2023-043.quote: use the order of operations to find the value of expressions with exponents
g6-2023-043.why: The item evaluates 7 × (5−3)^3 − 20 ÷ 4. The Row Game rows have the same shape — a product with an exponent plus or minus a second term — and are worked by the order of operations.

g6-2024-014.quote: students extend their understanding of the order of operations to include expressions with
g6-2024-014.why: The item is 8^2 ÷ 4 × 2^3: the powers must be found before the multiplication and division. Jada and Noah argue over exactly that in 6 · 10^2, one squaring first and one multiplying first.

g6-2025-019.quote: Find the value of the expressions in one of the columns.
g6-2025-019.why: The item evaluates (3^2 + 5·3)/2^3, with exponents in both numerator and denominator. The Row Game asks for the value of exactly this kind of multi-operation expression with exponents.

g6-2025-040.quote: Jada says the total volume is 27,000 cubic inches. Noah says it is
g6-2025-040.why: The item is 4(3 + 5^2) − 6, whose trap is adding 3 + 5 before squaring. The Cool-down is that error exactly: Jada computes (20 + 10)^3 while Noah computes 20 + 10^3.

g6-2026-045.quote: Find the value of the expressions in one of the columns.
g6-2026-045.why: The item evaluates 3(4^3 − 6^2) + 7(2 + 1)^3 — two groupings, three powers. The Row Game is the only place students are asked to find the values of expressions with exponents at this level of nesting.

g6-2023-012.quote: Circle the expression that represents the number of inches the plant grew
g6-2023-012.why: The item asks which expression is "14 less than the product of 8 and y," where the trap is writing 14 − 8y. The Cool-down makes students choose between x − 8 and 8 − x for a "grew by" comparison — the same order-of-subtraction decision.

g6-2024-002.quote: Write expressions to show Clare’s age when her cousin is at different ages.
g6-2024-002.why: The item asks for "5 more than the product of 2 and y" (2y + 5). This activity builds exactly those two pieces: x + 5 for "5 years older" and 3n for "3 times as many."

g6-2025-030.quote: Another esport player scored p fewer points than Priya. Write an expression
g6-2025-030.why: The item wants "the sum of fifteen and five less than twice a number n" — 15 + (2n − 5). This activity writes a comparison expression with a variable (473 − p), but nothing in grade 6 nests two operations inside one phrase, which is why confidence is low and the item’s p-value is 0.26.

g6-2026-030.quote: students relate quantities in situations to numerical and variable expressions
g6-2026-030.why: The item wants "55 less than the sum of 4 and twice a number c" — (4 + 2c) − 55. The activity practises the "fewer than" ordering with a variable, but again only one operation at a time.

g6-2023-018.quote: using mathematical vocabulary related to expressions, such as “coefficient,” “variable,” and “exponent.”
g6-2023-018.why: The item asks for the coefficient of the variable in 5z + (9 ÷ 3). This is the only grade 6 activity in which students are expected to use the word "coefficient"; no grade 6 task actually asks a student to name the coefficient of an expression.

g6-2025-023.quote: when considering the difference between expressions like 3 x and 3x
g6-2025-023.why: The item asks for the coefficient in 2x^3, where the distractor is the exponent 3. The activity is built on telling 3^x from 3x and uses "coefficient" and "exponent" as the words for that difference.

g6-2026-038.quote: practice using mathematical vocabulary related to expressions, such as “coefficient,”
g6-2026-038.why: The item asks for the coefficient in 6n^5. Same activity, same discrimination between the number in front and the number above; the vocabulary is named in the Activity Synthesis rather than practised in a task.

g6-2023-022.quote: They evaluate expressions when given a value for the variable.
g6-2023-022.why: The item evaluates 5b + c^3 at b = 7, c = 4. The activity is a list of expressions with exponents and coefficients to evaluate at a given value of the variable.

g6-2025-005.quote: Find the value of each expression for the given value of x
g6-2025-005.why: The item evaluates c^3 + 4h − 7 at c = 2, h = 3. The Cool-down is the same task — 4 + x^2, 4^x, 4x at a given value — and is where the curriculum tests it.

g6-2026-004.quote: they also deepen their understanding of the order of operations
g6-2026-004.why: The item evaluates 2(12 − x) + y^2 at x = 7, y = 3, so a substitution has to be followed through parentheses and a power. This activity is where substitution and the order of operations are worked together.

g6-2023-035.activity: Writing Equivalent Expressions Using the Distributive Property
g6-2023-035.quote: use the distributive property to write an equivalent expression
g6-2023-035.why: The item expands 4(3m + 1). The activity’s table contains 3(2x + 1) as a row to be rewritten as a sum — the same task with the same shape. Lesson 11 is marked optional in the pacing guide, so a class may never have done it; the non-optional runner-up is Lesson 10, Activity "Areas of Partitioned Rectangles," where the same product-and-sum pair is written for a rectangle’s area.

g6-2023-024.activity: Writing Equivalent Expressions Using the Distributive Property
g6-2023-024.quote: students generate equivalent algebraic expressions using the distributive property
g6-2023-024.why: The item needs 8(2a + 3b) − 2b = 16a + 22b: distribute over two unlike terms, then collect the b terms. The distributing half is this activity (y(3x + 4z) is a row); the collecting half is not asked anywhere in grade 6. Optional lesson; non-optional runner-up is Lesson 10, "Areas of Partitioned Rectangles."

g6-2026-019.activity: Writing Equivalent Expressions Using the Distributive Property
g6-2026-019.quote: They practice writing a sum or difference when given a product
g6-2026-019.why: The item needs 5(6m + 3) + 4m = 34m + 15, again distribute-then-collect. Only the distributing step is practised here, and in an optional lesson; non-optional runner-up is Lesson 10, "Areas of Partitioned Rectangles."

g6-2024-041.quote: Select all the expressions that represent the large rectangle’s total area.
g6-2024-041.why: The item asks why 6 + 8x is not equivalent to 3(3 + 5x) and wants a correct equivalent. This Cool-down asks students to separate correct distributions (5(b + 3), 5b + 15) from a plausible wrong one (3(5 + b)) for the same rectangle.

g6-2026-032.activity: Writing Equivalent Expressions Using the Distributive Property
g6-2026-032.quote: a product when given a sum or difference
g6-2026-032.why: The item factors 24x + 18y into 6(4x + 3y). This activity’s table runs in that direction too (4x − 20, 10x − 5 must be written as products). Optional lesson; the non-optional runner-up is Lesson 10, Activity "Partitioned Rectangles When Lengths Are Unknown," where 8 · 5 + 5x is rewritten as the product 5(8 + x).

g6-2024-003.quote: a number that can be used in place of the variable to make
g6-2024-003.why: The item asks which value of b makes 3b > 12 true. This is the activity that defines a solution to an inequality as a value that makes it true and has students decide whether given heights qualify.

g6-2025-027.quote: Select all numbers that are solutions to the inequality w < 1 .
g6-2025-027.why: The item asks which number is NOT a solution to 3w ≥ 12. The Cool-down is the same sorting of candidate values into solutions and non-solutions of a given inequality.

g6-2026-026.quote: determining whether a value is a solution to one or more of the
g6-2026-026.why: The item asks which value of k makes k − 16 > 29 true. Deciding whether a particular number satisfies a stated inequality is precisely the reasoning in the ride-height questions.

g6-2024-022.quote: Write expressions that can show how many comic books Diego has for different
g6-2024-022.why: The item wants 3s − 4 for "4 fewer than 3 times the number of stamps Tammy has." This activity writes 3n for "3 times as many comic books" and x + 5 for an age comparison; the item combines the two steps.

g6-2026-006.activity: Every Cube in the Whole World
g6-2026-006.quote: students develop the formulas for the surface area and the volume of a
g6-2026-006.why: The item adds six side lengths, two of them containing x, to get 2x + 18 for a perimeter. This activity is the one place students build an expression for a figure’s total measurement from its parts with a variable edge length and collect like terms; no grade 6 activity writes a perimeter expression with variables.

g6-2023-040.activity: Partitioned Rectangles When Lengths Are Unknown
g6-2023-040.quote: students use expressions with variables to represent lengths of sides and areas
g6-2023-040.why: The item composes a square, a 3x-by-x rectangle and a square into one rectangle and solves 12x = 60 from its perimeter. Composing rectangles with an unknown side and writing expressions for the composite is this activity; writing a perimeter expression and solving back for the unknown is not asked anywhere in grade 6, which fits the item’s p-value of 0.13.

g6-2024-036.quote: The purpose of this activity is for students to practice solving equations.
g6-2024-036.why: The item is 25h = 62.50, a px = q equation with a non-whole-number solution. The Row Game columns include 6x = 45 and 8x = 60, which are the same equation type with the same kind of answer.

g6-2024-038.quote: Solve each equation. Explain or show your reasoning.
g6-2024-038.why: The item asks for the value of n making n/8 = 17 true. The Cool-down is three equations of the forms x + p = q and px = q to be solved, including a fractional-coefficient one.

g6-2025-046.quote: practice matching equations to situations and then solving those equations using their choice
g6-2025-046.why: The item asks students to write and solve an equation twice — 9 · 2x = 54 for the rug and 7p = 784 for the price. This activity is write-or-choose-then-solve for situations of exactly the px = q shape (the solar-panel question is 1.5p = 100).

g6-2026-027.quote: students select an equation with a variable that can represent a situation with
g6-2026-027.why: The item asks which equation determines the number of sugar-cookie boxes, x + 250 = 324. Storytime is three situations against six candidate equations, including the x + 5 = 20 versus x + 20 = 5 confusion the distractors exploit.

g6-2026-041.quote: Kiran scores 223 fewer points in a computer game than Mai.
g6-2026-041.why: The item asks students to write and solve an equation for "Dan has 43 fewer cards than Bella’s 150." The activity’s first question is the same sentence with different numbers, with the same competing equations to sort out.

g6-2023-030.quote: They represent this on the number line with a closed (include) or open
g6-2023-030.why: The item reads a number line with a closed circle at 2 and a leftward ray and asks which inequality it graphs. The card sort matches number lines to math statements and is where the closed/open circle convention is settled.

g6-2024-011.quote: Draw a number line to represent this inequality.
g6-2024-011.why: The item goes the other way — given x ≥ −3, pick its graph. The Cool-down asks students to draw the number line for a given inequality, though it uses a strict inequality, so the closed circle for ≥ has to come from Lesson 8.

g6-2025-038.quote: Match each story and question with 3 other representations.
g6-2025-038.why: The item shows a number line (closed circle at 15, ray to the right) and asks students to write the inequality in x. The card sort pairs each number line with its math statement, which is this translation.

g6-2026-023.quote: represent each height requirement on a number line
g6-2026-023.why: The item asks which number line shows "a rider must be at least 48 inches tall." The activity is amusement-park height requirements, including a "58 inches minimum," written as inequalities and graphed on number lines.

g6-2023-003.quote: Select all equations that can represent the relationship between b , cups of
g6-2023-003.why: The item asks which equation relates cookies c to days d at 450 per day. The Cool-down gives a constant-ratio table and asks which equations can represent the relationship between the two variables, with the reversed-variable distractors the item also uses.

g6-2023-046.quote: What point on the graph would represent the time it takes the robot
g6-2023-046.why: The item reads a graph of chores against money, asks for the relationship and the dependent and independent variables, then for the earnings at 9 chores. The Cool-down asks which variable is independent, what a plotted point means, and what point would represent a value off the plotted range.

g6-2024-042.quote: the terms “dependent variable” and “independent variable” are introduced to describe the
g6-2024-042.why: The item gives c = 2.75t and asks for the relationship and which variable is independent. This activity is where the two terms are introduced, on a relationship of exactly this form written as an equation in two variables.

g6-2025-041.quote: allows students to interpret and write equations with variables
g6-2025-041.why: The item gives a table of blocks of cheese against dollars and asks for an equation for t in terms of b plus the dependent and independent variables. This activity moves from a table of equivalent ratios to equations in two variables and names the two kinds of variable.

g6-2026-014.lessonTitle: Tables, Equations, and Graphs, Oh My!
g6-2026-014.quote: each student focuses on just one of those equations to learn about the
g6-2026-014.why: The item wants c = 15p + 5 — a rate plus a one-time fee. Every two-variable equation in grade 6, here and in Lessons 16–18, uses a single operation (E = 6s, G = J + 13); nothing in the course combines a rate with a constant, so this placement covers the interpreting-an-equation-for-a-situation demand only.
